title: Weekly Briefing: AI Agents Are Becoming a Second Job, Anthropic Bans Abuse of Claude, and OpenAI’s Revenue Gap Raises New Questions
author: Jacob Morgan
summary: Jacob Morgan's Future Ready Leadership weekly briefing picks three stories and adds his own commentary aimed at CHROs and senior people leaders. The first, from Business Insider and BCG data, shows that adopting AI agents has more than doubled but that supervising them creates a second job of correction, retraining and task switching, which Morgan reads as a job-design and workload issue. The second covers Anthropic's updated usage policy banning prolonged abuse of Claude, which Morgan uses to ask whether habits formed with machines spill over into how employees treat people. The third concerns Axios reporting that OpenAI's annualized revenue is about 20 billion dollars lower than widely reported because of accounting methodology. His lesson is to interrogate what any AI metric actually measures before celebrating it. The issue ends with a note on a podcast conversation with Jabil's CHRO.
points: AI agents can move work rather than remove it, so leaders should measure the management burden of supervising agents alongside any productivity gains.
Agent supervision is becoming a job-design question that touches workload, performance expectations, skills and compensation.
Norms for how employees speak to AI tools may shape workplace culture, so leaders should watch how human-AI habits carry over to human interactions.
Two technically accurate AI metrics can tell different stories depending on how they are calculated, as the OpenAI revenue gap shows.
Before celebrating an AI number, leaders should ask what was measured, against what baseline, over what period and whether it produced a real business outcome.
quotes: I think this is an important correction to the productivity conversation. AI can absolutely remove work, but it can also move work.
Instead of producing the output yourself, you may spend more time assigning tasks, checking quality, fixing mistakes, and deciding when the result is trustworthy enough to use.

For CHROs, that means agent adoption is becoming a job-design issue. If someone is supervising three, five, or ten agents, what happens to workload, performance expectations, skills, and compensation?

Do the habits people develop with machines spill over into how they communicate with people? We do not have a definitive answer yet, but leaders should probably pay attention to the norms forming around human-AI interaction.
Those numbers may all be technically accurate while still telling very different stories depending on how they are calculated.
Before celebrating an AI metric, ask what is underneath it. What was measured? Compared with what? Over what period? And did it translate into an actual business outcome?
